source_text:
Fragmenta in epistulam ad Hebraeos (in catenis)
Hebr: Prolog
Οἱ αἱρετικοί φασι μὴ εἶναι Παύλου τὴν ἐπιστολήν, καὶ τούτου πρώτην ἀπόδειξιν
προφέρουσι τὸ μὴ προτετάχθαι αὐτοῦ τὸ ὄνομα ὡς ἐν ταῖς ἄλλαις ἐπιστολαῖς·
δεύτερον τὸ τὴν φράσιν ἄλλην εἶναι, τοῦτ' ἔστι ξένην παρὰ τὴν Παύλου καὶ τὴν
κατασκευήν. δεῖ τοίνυν εἰδέναι ὅτι Παῦλος ἐμισεῖτο ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων ὡς ἀποστασίαν
νόμου διδάσκων, διὰ τοῦτο καὶ κινδυνεύσας ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις καὶ μόλις διαφυγὼν
ἐπέμφθη εἰς Ῥώμην. ὠφέλιμα τοίνυν γράφων Ἑβραίοις οὐ προτίθησι τὸ ὄνομα
ἑαυτοῦ, ἵνα μὴ τῷ μίσει τῷ πρὸς αὐτὸν ζημιωθῶσι τὴν ὠφέλειαν τὴν ἀπὸ τῆς
ἐπιστολῆς. Γράφει δὲ αὐτοῖς ὥς φησιν ὁ μακάριος Σευηριανός τῇ Ἑβραίων γλώττῃ, ἃ
καὶ ἡρμηνεύθη ὑπό τινος τῶν μαθητῶν, ὑπὸ Λουκᾶ, ἢ μᾶλλον ὑπὸ Κλήμεντος οὗ καὶ
μέμνηται. διὰ τοῦτο ξένη φράσις. καὶ 346 τοῦτο ἐζήτηται τοῖς πρὸ ἡμῶν, καὶ
Εὐσέβιος ὁ Παμφίλου ἱστορικώτερος γεγονὼς τῶν πρὸ αὐτοῦ καὶ μετ' αὐτοῦ,
ἐμνημόνευσε τῆς ζητήσεως, καὶ ὅτι τοῖς πατράσιν ἡμῶν τοῖς παλαιοῖς τῶν
ἐπισκόπων ἔδοξε Παύλου τὴν ἐπιστολὴν εἶναι. Hebr 1,1–2 Πολυμερῶς μὲν κατὰ τὰς
διαφορὰς τῶν χρόνων ἐν αἷς ᾠκονομήθη τὰ περὶ ἡμῶν, οἷον ἐν τῇ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ γενέσει,
ἐν τοῖς κατὰ τὸν Κάϊν, ἐν τοῖς κατὰ τὸν Νῶε, ἐν τοῖς κατὰ τὸν Ἀβραάμ, ἐν τοῖς πρὸ
νόμου, ἐν τοῖς μετὰ νόμον· πολλὰ γὰρ τὰ μέρη τῆς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν τοῦ θεοῦ διοικήσεως.
πολυτρόπως δέ, ὅτι ἄλλη ἐδόθη ἐντολὴ τῷ Ἀδάμ, ἄλλη τῷ Νῶε, ἑτέρα τῷ Ἀβραάμ,
καὶ διὰ Μωϋσέως ἄλλη, καὶ διὰ τῶν προφητῶν διάφοροι. Ἐλάλησεν ἡμῖν ἐν υἱῷ,
ἀντὶ τοῦ δι' υἱοῦ· οὐ γὰρ ἐν αὐτῷ ὡς ἐν ὀργάνῳ, ἀλλὰ δι' αὐτοῦ ὡς οἰκονομοῦντος
σάρκα, ἵν' ἐντεῦθεν ἀρξαμένη τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἡ ἀκοή, καὶ ὥσπερ δραξαμένη ψηλαφίᾳ
τινὶ τοῦ λόγου οὕτως ἀναχθῇ εἰς τὴν προαιώνιον ὕπαρξιν. πρότερον γὰρ εἰρηκώς·
ἐλάλησεν ἡμῖν ἐν υἱῷ ὃν καὶ κληρονόμον ἔθηκεν –ἀντὶ τοῦ ἐποίησεν–, ἀνήγαγε τὸν
λόγον εἰς τὴν προαιώνιον ὕπαρξιν. καὶ τοῦτο ποιεῖ συνεχῶς, πῆ μὲν ἀνιὼν εἰς τὴν
θεολογίαν, πῆ δὲ κατιὼν εἰς τὴν ἐνανθρώπησιν. Hebr 1,3α Ζητῶν παραστῆσαι
τρανότερον τὸ ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας τοῦ πατρὸς γεγεννῆσθαι τὸν λόγον, τοῦ ἀπαυγάσματος
ἐμνημόνευσεν· τὸ γὰρ ἀπαύγασμα ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας ἐστὶν ἐκείνου οὗ ἐστιν ἀπαύγασμα,
καὶ διηνεκὲς καὶ ἐξ αὐτοῦ καὶ οὐδέποτ' ἄνευ ἐκείνου ἐπινοούμενον οὗ ἐστιν
ἀπαύγασμα. ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ τὸ ἀπαύγασμα ἐλάττονα δείκνυσι τὴν φύσιν παρ' ἐκεῖνο οὗ
ἐστιν ἀπαύγασμα καὶ οὐκ ἐν ἰδίᾳ ὑποστάσει, ἑτέρᾳ λέξει τοῦτο παρέστησεν εἰπών·
καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως, τὸ μὲν πρῶτον τεθεικὼς εἰς ἀπόδειξιν τοῦ ἐκ τῆς
οὐσίας ἀμερῶς εἶναι, τὸ δὲ δεύτερον, ὅτι οὐκ ἀνυπόστατον. ὥσπερ γὰρ Ἰωάννης
λόγον ὀνομάσας ἐπήγαγε· πρὸς θεὸν ἦν καὶ θεὸς ἦν, οὕτω καὶ Παῦλος ἀπαύγασμα
εἰπὼν προσέθηκεν· καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως. 347 Hebr 1,3β Τοῦτό ἐστιν ὃ λέγει
Ἰερεμίας· ἰσχυρὰ ἔργα λόγων αὐτοῦ. Hebr 1,3ξ Εἰ καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, ἀλλ' οὖν
ἐν δόξῃ καὶ φύσει τῆς θεότητος ἦν καὶ τῶν ὑπερτάτων τοῦ θεοῦ πατρὸς οὐκ ἀπέστη
θρόνων· καὶ ἠλαττωμένου βραχὺ παρ' ἀγγέλους διὰ τὸ τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος μέτρον–
pass_a_gloss:
[Edition heading: Fragments on the letter to the Hebrews (in the catenas). Hebrews: prologue.]
The heretics say that the letter is not Paul's, and as first proof of this they bring forward that his name has not been placed at the front, as in the other letters; second, that the phrasing is other, that is, foreign compared with Paul's, and (so is) the composition. One must know, then, that Paul was hated by the Jews as teaching apostasy from the law; for this reason too, having been in danger in Jerusalem and having barely escaped, he was sent to Rome. Writing useful things to the Hebrews, then, he does not set his own name in front, so that they might not, by the hatred toward him, be deprived of the benefit from the letter. And he writes to them, as the blessed Severian says, in the language of the Hebrews, which (writings) were also translated by one of the disciples, by Luke, or rather by Clement, whom he also mentions. For this reason the phrasing is foreign. And this has been inquired into by those before us, and Eusebius (son/disciple) of Pamphilus, having been more of a historian than those before him and after him, mentioned the inquiry, and that it seemed to our fathers, the ancient ones of the bishops, that the letter is Paul's.
Hebrews 1:1-2. "In many parts," according to the differences of the times in which the things concerning us were arranged, such as in the creation of Adam, in the things concerning Cain, in the things concerning Noah, in the things concerning Abraham, in the things before the law, in the things after the law; for many are the parts of God's management on our behalf. And "in many ways," because one commandment was given to Adam, another to Noah, another to Abraham, and another through Moses, and different ones through the prophets. "He spoke to us in a Son," in place of "through a Son"; for not in him as in an instrument, but through him as administering flesh, so that the hearing of the Jews, beginning from there and as it were having grasped the Word by a kind of touching, might thus be led up to his existence before the ages. For having said first: "he spoke to us in a Son, whom he also appointed heir" (in place of "made"), he led the discourse up to the existence before the ages. And he does this constantly, at one point going up to theology, at another coming down to the becoming human.
Hebrews 1:3a. Seeking to present more clearly that the Word has been begotten from the essence of the Father, he mentioned the radiance; for the radiance is from the essence of that of which it is the radiance, and (is) continuous and from it and never conceived without that of which it is the radiance. But since the radiance shows a lesser nature than that of which it is the radiance, and not in its own subsistence, he presented this with another word, saying: "and stamp of the subsistence," having put the first as proof of being from the essence without division, and the second (to show) that he is not without subsistence. For just as John, having named (him) Word, added: "he was with God and was God," so also Paul, having said radiance, added: "and stamp of the subsistence."
Hebrews 1:3b. This is what Jeremiah says: "strong (are the) works of his words."
Hebrews 1:3 (label printed '1,3ξ', third part of the verse). Even if the Word became flesh, yet he was in the glory and nature of the godhead and did not stand away from the highest thrones of God the Father; and (though he was) made a little lower than angels because of the measure of humanity [continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: Preface to Hebrews: The heretics say that this letter is not Paul’s. Their first proof is that his name is not placed at the head of it, as it is in his other letters. Their second is that its style is different, that is, foreign to Paul’s, and so is the way it is put together. We must understand, then, that Paul was hated by the Jews as a man who taught people to abandon the law (Acts 21:21). That is why he was in danger in Jerusalem, barely escaped, and was sent to Rome. So when he wrote something for the good of the Hebrews, he did not put his name at the head of it, so that their hatred of him would not rob them of the benefit of the letter. As the blessed Severian says, he wrote to them in the Hebrew language, and his words were translated by one of his disciples, by Luke, or more likely by Clement, whom he also mentions. That is why the style is foreign. Those before us also looked into this question. Eusebius, the disciple of Pamphilus, who was more of a historian than anyone before or after him, recorded the inquiry, and recorded too that our fathers, the bishops of old, held the letter to be Paul’s.

On Hebrews 1:1–2: “In many parts” refers to the different times in which God arranged our affairs: at the creation of Adam, in the time of Cain, in the time of Noah, in the time of Abraham, before the law and after the law. God’s governance on our behalf has many parts. “In many ways”, because one commandment was given to Adam, another to Noah, another to Abraham, another through Moses, and various commandments through the prophets. “He spoke to us in a Son” stands for “through a Son”: not in him as in an instrument, but through him as the one who carried out his saving work in the flesh. In this way the Jews could begin to listen from there, grasp the Word as if by touch, and so be led up to his existence before the ages. For having first said, “He spoke to us in a Son, whom he also appointed heir” (“appointed” stands for “made”), he raised his discourse to the Son’s existence before the ages. He does this all the time: now he rises to speak of Christ as God, now he comes down to his becoming man.

On Hebrews 1:3: He wanted to show more clearly that the Word was begotten from the Father’s essence, so he spoke of radiance. Radiance comes from the essence of that whose radiance it is; it is continuous with it, it comes from it, and it can never be thought of apart from it. But radiance suggests a nature lesser than that whose radiance it is, and one with no subsistence of its own. So he expressed the point with a second word, saying, “and the exact stamp of his subsistence”. The first word he set down to prove that the Son is from the Father’s essence without division; the second, to show that he is not without a subsistence of his own. Just as John named him “Word” and then added, “he was with God, and he was God” (John 1:1), so Paul said “radiance” and then added, “and the exact stamp of his subsistence”.
On Hebrews 1:3: This is what Jeremiah says: “Mighty are the works of his words” (Joel 2:11).

On Hebrews 1:3: Even though the Word became flesh (John 1:14), he remained in the glory and nature of the Godhead and never left the highest thrones of God the Father. And although he was “made a little lower than the angels” (Hebrews 2:9) because of the measure of humanity …

choices.why: Edition label for the introductory note, rendered once as a lead-in.
The catena compiler's own words, naming Severian as his source; kept as written.
Conventional sense of the genitive (Eusebius 'of Pamphilus'), not his father.
The old English 'more grandly' and 'purely' missed both words.
The edition splits verse 3 into parts a, b and c ('ξ' is a misprint for γ: the note is on 'sat down at the right hand'); each part keeps its own paragraph and the English label 1:3.

choices.english: This is what Jeremiah says: “Mighty are the works of his words” (Joel 2:11).
choices.why: The words are the Septuagint of Joel 2:11 (ὅτι ἰσχυρὰ ἔργα λόγων αὐτοῦ); the Greek names Jeremiah and that is kept. The old '(Jeremiah 32:27)' does not contain these words.

choices.english: although he was “made a little lower than the angels” (Hebrews 2:9)
choices.why: Wording of Hebrews 2:9 (Psalm 8:5); the old 'abased briefly by the angels' reversed the sense of παρά.
rejected: being abased briefly by the angels (old)
